answers.java_tx_design: On our tax-assessment service, I ran into a boundary problem processing refund calculations. Originally the whole assessment -- validate the return, compute the refund, write the refund record, and call our internal audit-flagging service -- ran in one @Transactional method. During the March filing surge, when we process about 40,000 returns a day instead of the usual 5,000, transactions blocked on the same taxpayer_accounts row for up to 600ms whenever the audit-flagging call was slow. I moved the audit call outside the transaction: the assessment and refund write commit together, since those two must be atomic, and I write a queued 'needs audit check' row in the same transaction instead of calling out synchronously. Assessment latency at p99 dropped from about 1.4 seconds to 220ms during peak. The failure I hit afterward: the audit queue itself backed up 3,000 rows deep during one surge because I hadn't sized its consumer for peak volume, so I added a second consumer instance.
answers.java_ops: We had connection pool exhaustion on the same service during that same March surge, before I made the transaction fix. HikariCP wait times hit 900ms at p95, and I pulled pool metrics from Grafana showing all 25 connections were in use for stretches of 2-3 seconds at a time, correlated with the slow audit calls I mentioned. Before I understood the root cause, my first move was just raising pool size from 25 to 50, which briefly helped the wait metric but pushed our database's own connection limit close to its ceiling of 200 total across all services, so I reverted that within a day. The actual fix was the transaction-boundary change, which reduced how long connections were held per request; after that, pool wait dropped to under 30ms at p95 even at the same peak volume, without needing more connections at all.
answers.rust_readiness: I haven't written Rust, in production or otherwise, so I want to be upfront about that rather than talk around it. If I were building a realistic plan, I'd start with the official book and Rustlings over the first month, alongside rewriting something small I already understand well -- probably our refund-calculation logic, since I know its edge cases from having built it in Java -- to force myself to hit ownership and borrowing for real. I'd expect the first two months to be mostly fighting the compiler on things that are simple in Java, and I wouldn't feel ready to own a production boundary until I'd built at least one real async service end to end, maybe four to six months in. On migration generally, I'd want to move a small, stateless, well-tested piece first and run it alongside the Java version rather than trust a rewrite immediately, which is closer to how I approach any risky change, language aside.
answers.rust_boundary: Without Rust experience myself, I'd still apply the same approach I used moving the audit-flagging call out of our transaction: find the least stateful, most isolated piece of the write path first, something like fee or interest calculation that takes inputs and returns a number without needing to touch the database directly, and put that behind an interface the Java side calls. I'd run it in parallel with the existing Java calculation for some weeks, logging both results, and only cut over once outputs matched consistently. What I'd watch: latency of the new call, error rate, and a count of any mismatches against the Java result. I don't have my own experience carving this particular kind of boundary in Rust, so I'd want a more experienced Rust engineer to sanity-check the interface design before I trusted my own judgment on it fully.
answers.money_correctness: On TaxCore, every refund disbursement carries an idempotency key made from the taxpayer's filing ID plus the tax year, enforced with a unique constraint in a disbursements table, so a retried disbursement request after a timeout returns the existing record instead of issuing a second payment. This broke about three years ago: our payment processor's callback endpoint started timing out under load during a surge, and our retry logic resent 85 disbursement requests over about five hours with a bug that generated a new filing-ID-plus-year key each time, due to a data-type mismatch in how the tax year was formatted between two of our internal services. I found it during our weekly reconciliation, which showed 85 taxpayers with two disbursement records instead of one, totaling about $142,000 in duplicate payments. I corrected each with a reversing entry, not a deletion, and fixed the formatting mismatch so key generation was consistent across both services.
answers.incident_response: Separately, we had an incident where a batch job that applies interest to overdue tax balances ran twice for the same night because a scheduler misconfiguration after a deployment left two scheduled triggers active instead of one. It affected about 6,000 accounts with double-applied interest, averaging $3.20 extra per account. I noticed it the next morning from an anomaly in our daily accrual-total dashboard, which showed roughly double the expected interest applied, and had the affected account list scoped by 10 a.m. and a reversing-entry fix deployed by 2 p.m. the same day. I told my lead and our operations contact as soon as I suspected the double-run, before I'd finished scoping it, since taxpayer-facing statements go out the next day and needed to be held. The postmortem's change was adding a check at job startup that fails loudly if another instance is already running, which we verified by intentionally triggering a double-run in staging afterward.
answers.process_skipping: During the interest-double-application incident, I was tempted to skip the normal review step and push the scheduler fix immediately once I found it, since statements were going out that evening. I didn't skip it: I posted in our team channel, got a colleague to review the one-line scheduler config change over a ten-minute call instead of our usual next-day review cycle, and got it merged and deployed within that window. I think the key thing that made review possible even under time pressure was that the fix itself was small and easy to reason about quickly, which isn't always true. I'd only consider actually skipping review if getting even a fast second opinion were genuinely impossible and real harm were actively accumulating, and I'd want to announce that decision and log it clearly rather than quietly doing it and explaining later, which I haven't personally had to do.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: I once shipped a rounding change to how we calculate late-payment penalties that was technically correct but changed the result for about 200 existing draft assessments in a way I hadn't checked before deploying. I found the discrepancy myself the next day while spot-checking an unrelated ticket, and reported it to my lead that same afternoon along with the affected count, rather than waiting to see if anyone else noticed first. On on-call: I've been on our rotation for about five years, one week in six, and I handle taxpayer-facing incident escalations directly rather than just paging someone else. I also mentor one junior engineer currently, mostly through code review and walking through incidents like the scheduler one together after the fact, and I've never seen on-call or that kind of mentoring time as separate from the actual engineering work.
answers.evidence_decision: About two years ago, a colleague proposed rewriting our refund-calculation module from scratch, arguing the existing code was too hard to follow. I disagreed with a full rewrite and instead pulled our incident history, showing we'd had exactly one bug in that module in three years, plus an estimate of the two to three months a rewrite would take against other backlog work. The team discussed it and decided against the full rewrite, opting instead for me to refactor the module's worst-documented section incrementally over a few weeks while leaving the rest alone. I did that refactor as agreed and didn't go back and quietly rewrite the rest of it afterward, even though I still think parts of it could be cleaner, because the team's call was that the risk of a rewrite wasn't worth it for code that wasn't actually causing problems.
answers.own_contribution: In the disbursement idempotency-key fix I described, tracing the formatting mismatch between the two services and designing the corrected key format was my own work; a colleague on the payments-integration side implemented the change on their service's end once I'd specified what the key needed to look like. For the scheduler-duplication incident, scoping the 6,000 affected accounts and writing the reversing-entry logic was mine; the actual startup-check code that prevents a future double-run was written by another engineer on my team from a short design note I wrote, since he was already deep in that part of the codebase and could move faster than I could there. I think it's worth naming that split rather than saying 'we fixed it,' since the diagnosis and the fix design were mine specifically, and the implementation of the prevention measure wasn't.
answers.java_recovery: The 85-disbursement duplicate-payment issue is my clearest recovery example. I scoped it with a query joining disbursements against filing_id and tax_year, grouping to find any pair with matching taxpayer and year but different disbursement IDs, which is how I got the exact count of 85 and confirmed the $142,000 total. For each one I checked the payment processor's own transaction log to be sure both payments had actually gone out, since I didn't want to assume every flagged pair was a real duplicate. I fixed each with a reversing disbursement entry dated to the discovery date, then re-ran our weekly reconciliation manually against just those 85 filing IDs afterward to confirm balances matched. My first assumption was that the bug affected any retried disbursement, but once I checked timestamps I found it only hit requests retried during that specific five-hour window when the callback timeouts were happening, which narrowed the blast radius considerably.
answers.java_perf_change: Our return-status lookup endpoint, which taxpayers hit through the public portal, sat at p99 of 1.8 seconds during filing season against a target of 500ms. I measured with a profiler and found we were doing a join across three tables for every lookup when only one was actually needed for the common case of checking status, the others were pulled for an edit-history feature almost nobody used on that screen. My first attempt was caching the whole response, which helped average latency but did little for p99, since most lookups were for accounts filed within the last day and rarely repeated. What worked was splitting the query so the common status-only case skipped the two unused joins entirely, dropping p99 to about 240ms. I kept the full query available behind a separate, explicit endpoint for the edit-history feature so I wasn't removing functionality, just not paying its cost on every request.
answers.rust_hands_on: I haven't written any Rust code, production or personal, so I don't have a real answer here beyond saying so plainly. I've read a bit about ownership and the borrow checker out of general interest, but I haven't sat down and actually hit a compiler error myself, which I think is a meaningfully different thing from having done it.
answers.rust_when_not: Without hands-on Rust experience, I'd still say I wouldn't move anything that's actively changing or poorly understood by the team maintaining it, since a rewrite needs stability to verify against, and our own team is entirely Java-focused right now. On holding back a rewrite urge specifically in Rust, I don't have that experience, but I have held back a rewrite urge in Java: I wanted to rewrite our refund-calculation module, which I described in the evidence-decision question, and the team's data on incident history convinced me it wasn't worth the risk. I think the same reasoning would apply to a Rust rewrite if I were ever tempted -- measure whether there's a real problem first, rather than assume a new language would fix something that isn't actually broken.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: During a quarterly reconciliation about two years ago, our totals were off by $890 across roughly 3,000 refund disbursements for the quarter, small per-account but consistent enough that I didn't write it off as noise. I traced it to how we handled partial refunds for taxpayers who'd filed an amended return after their original refund had already gone out -- the amendment logic recalculated the full refund amount and disbursed the difference, but for eleven cases a second amendment arrived before the first amendment's disbursement had settled, so the second amendment's calculation was based on stale data. I corrected those eleven with adjusting entries based on recalculating from the final settled state, not the intermediate one, and added a check that blocks a new amendment calculation from starting until the prior one's disbursement confirms as settled. My first guess was a currency-rounding issue, since $890 across 3,000 looked small enough to be that, and I ruled it out only after checking each case's timeline individually.
answers.prod_data_verification: I've wanted to check something against real production balances more than once, most clearly during the disbursement duplicate-payment issue, and what I did was take that week's disbursements and filing records, strip taxpayer names and account numbers, and run my grouping query against that masked copy in a separate database rather than live. For the scheduler-duplication incident, where I needed to confirm the startup check actually prevented a second run under real conditions, I tested that in staging by deliberately triggering a duplicate scheduler trigger there, rather than trying to reproduce it in production at all. The one time I checked a live number directly was confirming the $3.20-per-account average from the interest incident, which I did with a read-only query and mentioned in our incident channel before running it, since I wanted the number for the postmortem rather than to change anything.
